source: Call me Ishmael. Some years ago—never mind how long precisely—having little or no money in my purse, and nothing particular to interest me on shore, I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world. It is a way I have of driving off the spleen and regulating the circulation. Whenever I find myself growing grim about the mouth; whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever I find myself involuntarily pausing before coffin warehouses, and bringing up the rear of every funeral I meet; and especially whenever my hypos get such an upper hand of me, that it requires a strong moral principle to prevent me from deliberately stepping into the street, and methodically knocking people’s hats off—then, I account it high time to get to sea as soon as I can. This is my substitute for pistol and ball. With a philosophical flourish Cato throws himself upon his sword; I quietly take to the ship. There is nothing surprising in this. If they but knew it, almost all men in their degree, some time or other, cherish very nearly the same feelings towards the ocean with me.

There now is your insular city of the Manhattoes, belted round by wharves as Indian isles by coral reefs—commerce surrounds it with her surf. Right and left, the streets take you waterward. Its extreme downtown is the battery, where that noble mole is washed by waves, and cooled by breezes, which a few hours previous were out of sight of land. Look at the crowds of water-gazers there.

Circumambulate the city of a dreamy Sabbath afternoon. Go from Corlears Hook to Coenties Slip, and from thence, by Whitehall, northward. What do you see?—Posted like silent sentinels all around the town, stand thousands upon thousands of mortal men fixed in ocean reveries. Some leaning against the spiles; some seated upon the pier-heads; some looking over the bulwarks of ships from China; some high aloft in the rigging, as if striving to get a still better seaward peep. But these are all landsmen; of week days pent up in lath and plaster—tied to counters, nailed to benches, clinched to desks. How then is this? Are the green fields gone? What do they here?

But look! here come more crowds, pacing straight for the water, and seemingly bound for a dive. Strange! Nothing will content them but the extremest limit of the land; loitering under the shady lee of yonder warehouses will not suffice. No. They must get just as nigh the water as they possibly can without falling in. And there they stand—miles of them—leagues. Inlanders all, they come from lanes and alleys, streets and avenues—north, east, south, and west. Yet here they all unite. Tell me, does the magnetic virtue of the needles of the compasses of all those ships attract them thither?

Once more. Say you are in the country; in some high land of lakes. Take almost any path you please, and ten to one it carries you down in a dale, and leaves you there by a pool in the stream. There is magic in it. Let the most absent-minded of men be plunged in his deepest reveries—stand that man on his legs, set his feet a-going, and he will infallibly lead you to water, if water there be in all that region. Should you ever be athirst in the great American desert, try this experiment, if your caravan happen to be supplied with a metaphysical professor. Yes, as every one knows, meditation and water are wedded for ever.

But here is an artist. He desires to paint you the dreamiest, shadiest, quietest, most enchanting bit of romantic landscape in all the valley of the Saco. What is the chief element he employs? There stand his trees, each with a hollow trunk, as if a hermit and a crucifix were within; and here sleeps his meadow, and there sleep his cattle; and up from yonder cottage goes a sleepy smoke. Deep into distant woodlands winds a mazy way, reaching to overlapping spurs of mountains bathed in their hill-side blue. But though the picture lies thus tranced, and though this pine-tree shakes down its sighs like leaves upon this shepherd’s head, yet all were vain, unless the shepherd’s eye were fixed upon the magic stream before him. Go visit the Prairies in June, when for scores on scores of miles you wade knee-deep among Tiger-lilies—what is the one charm wanting?—Water—there is not a drop of water there! Were Niagara but a cataract of sand, would you travel your thousand miles to see it? Why did the poor poet of Tennessee, upon suddenly receiving two handfuls of silver, deliberate whether to buy him a coat, which he sadly needed, or invest his money in a pedestrian trip to Rockaway Beach? Why is almost every robust healthy boy with a robust healthy soul in him, at some time or other crazy to go to sea? Why upon your first voyage as a passenger, did you yourself feel such a mystical vibration, when first told that you and your ship were now out of sight of land? Why did the old Persians hold the sea holy? Why did the Greeks give it a separate deity, and own brother of Jove? Surely all this is not without meaning. And still deeper the meaning of that story of Narcissus, who because he could not grasp the tormenting, mild image he saw in the fountain, plunged into it and was drowned. But that same image, we ourselves see in all rivers and oceans. It is the image of the ungraspable phantom of life; and this is the key to it all.

Now, when I say that I am in the habit of going to sea whenever I begin to grow hazy about the eyes, and begin to be over conscious of my lungs, I do not mean to have it inferred that I ever go to sea as a passenger. For to go as a passenger you must needs have a purse, and a purse is but a rag unless you have something in it. Besides, passengers get sea-sick—grow quarrelsome—don’t sleep of nights—do not enjoy themselves much, as a general thing;—no, I never go as a passenger; nor, though I am something of a salt, do I ever go to sea as a Commodore, or a Captain, or a Cook. I abandon the glory and distinction of such offices to those who like them. For my part, I abominate all honorable respectable toils, trials, and tribulations of every kind whatsoever. It is quite as much as I can do to take care of myself, without taking care of ships, barques, brigs, schooners, and what not. And as for going as cook,—though I confess there is considerable glory in that, a cook being a sort of officer on ship-board—yet, somehow, I never fancied broiling fowls;—though once broiled, judiciously buttered, and judgmatically salted and peppered, there is no one who will speak more respectfully, not to say reverentially, of a broiled fowl than I will. It is out of the idolatrous dotings of the old Egyptians upon broiled ibis and roasted river horse, that you see the mummies of those creatures in their huge bake-houses the pyramids.

No, when I go to sea, I go as a simple sailor, right before the mast, plumb down into the forecastle, aloft there to the royal mast-head. True, they rather order me about some, and make me jump from spar to spar, like a grasshopper in a May meadow. And at first, this sort of thing is unpleasant enough. It touches one’s sense of honor, particularly if you come of an old established family in the land, the Van Rensselaers, or Randolphs, or Hardicanutes. And more than all, if just previous to putting your hand into the tar-pot, you have been lording it as a country schoolmaster, making the tallest boys stand in awe of you. The transition is a keen one, I assure you, from a schoolmaster to a sailor, and requires a strong decoction of Seneca and the Stoics to enable you to grin and bear it. But even this wears off in time.

What of it, if some old hunks of a sea-captain orders me to get a broom and sweep down the decks? What does that indignity amount to, weighed, I mean, in the scales of the New Testament? Do you think the archangel Gabriel thinks anything the less of me, because I promptly and respectfully obey that old hunks in that particular instance? Who ain’t a slave? Tell me that. Well, then, however the old sea-captains may order me about—however they may thump and punch me about, I have the satisfaction of knowing that it is all right; that everybody else is one way or other served in much the same way—either in a physical or metaphysical point of view, that is; and so the universal thump is passed round, and all hands should rub each other’s shoulder-blades, and be content.

Again, I always go to sea as a sailor, because they make a point of paying me for my trouble, whereas they never pay passengers a single penny that I ever heard of. On the contrary, passengers themselves must pay. And there is all the difference in the world between paying and being paid. The act of paying is perhaps the most uncomfortable infliction that the two orchard thieves entailed upon us. But being paid,—what will compare with it? The urbane activity with which a man receives money is really marvellous, considering that we so earnestly believe money to be the root of all earthly ills, and that on no account can a monied man enter heaven. Ah! how cheerfully we consign ourselves to perdition!

Finally, I always go to sea as a sailor, because of the wholesome exercise and pure air of the fore-castle deck. For as in this world, head winds are far more prevalent than winds from astern (that is, if you never violate the Pythagorean maxim), so for the most part the Commodore on the quarter-deck gets his atmosphere at second hand from the sailors on the forecastle. He thinks he breathes it first; but not so. In much the same way do the commonalty lead their leaders in many other things, at the same time that the leaders little suspect it. But wherefore it was that after having repeatedly smelt the sea as a merchant sailor, I should now take it into my head to go on a whaling voyage; this the invisible police officer of the Fates, who has the constant surveillance of me, and secretly dogs me, and influences me in some unaccountable way—he can better answer than any one else. And, doubtless, my going on this whaling voyage, formed part of the grand programme of Providence that was drawn up a long time ago. It came in as a sort of brief interlude and solo between more extensive performances. I take it that this part of the bill must have run something like this:
“Grand Contested Election for the Presidency of the United States. “WHALING VOYAGE BY ONE ISHMAEL. “BLOODY BATTLE IN AFFGHANISTAN.”

Though I cannot tell why it was exactly that those stage managers, the Fates, put me down for this shabby part of a whaling voyage, when others were set down for magnificent parts in high tragedies, and short and easy parts in genteel comedies, and jolly parts in farces—though I cannot tell why this was exactly; yet, now that I recall all the circumstances, I think I can see a little into the springs and motives which being cunningly presented to me under various disguises, induced me to set about performing the part I did, besides cajoling me into the delusion that it was a choice resulting from my own unbiased freewill and discriminating judgment.

Chief among these motives was the overwhelming idea of the great whale himself. Such a portentous and mysterious monster roused all my curiosity. Then the wild and distant seas where he rolled his island bulk; the undeliverable, nameless perils of the whale; these, with all the attending marvels of a thousand Patagonian sights and sounds, helped to sway me to my wish. With other men, perhaps, such things would not have been inducements; but as for me, I am tormented with an everlasting itch for things remote. I love to sail forbidden seas, and land on barbarous coasts. Not ignoring what is good, I am quick to perceive a horror, and could still be social with it—would they let me—since it is but well to be on friendly terms with all the inmates of the place one lodges in.

By reason of these things, then, the whaling voyage was welcome; the great flood-gates of the wonder-world swung open, and in the wild conceits that swayed me to my purpose, two and two there floated into my inmost soul, endless processions of the whale, and, mid most of them all, one grand hooded phantom, like a snow hill in the air.

Quite the reverse — passengers have to pay. And there is all the difference in the world between paying and being paid. Paying is perhaps the most uncomfortable punishment those two orchard thieves, Adam and Eve, left us with. But being paid — what can compare with that? The gracious readiness with which a man accepts money is truly remarkable, considering how earnestly we believe money is the root of all earthly evils, and that a moneyed man can on no account get into heaven. Ah, how cheerfully we sign ourselves over to damnation!

Finally, I always go to sea as a sailor because of the healthy exercise and pure air of the forecastle deck. For as in this world headwinds are far more common than winds from astern (that is, if you never violate the Pythagorean maxim), so for the most part the Commodore on the quarter-deck gets his air secondhand from the sailors on the forecastle. He thinks he breathes it first; but not so. In much the same way the common people lead their leaders in many other things, while the leaders little suspect it. But why it was that, after repeatedly smelling the sea as a merchant sailor, I should now take it into my head to go on a whaling voyage — that the invisible police officer of the Fates, who keeps me under constant surveillance, secretly dogs my steps, and influences me in some unaccountable way, can answer better than anyone else. And no doubt my going on this whaling voyage formed part of the grand program of Providence that was drawn up a long time ago. It came in as a sort of brief interlude and solo between more extensive performances. I take it that this part of the playbill must have run something like this:
"GRAND CONTESTED ELECTION FOR THE PRESIDENCY OF THE UNITED STATES." "WHALING VOYAGE BY ONE ISHMAEL." "BLOODY BATTLE IN AFFGHANISTAN."

Though I can't say exactly why those stage managers, the Fates, cast me in this shabby part of a whaling voyage, when others were given magnificent parts in high tragedies, short and easy parts in genteel comedies, and jolly parts in farces — though I can't say exactly why; still, now that I recall all the circumstances, I think I can see a little into the springs and motives that were cunningly presented to me under various disguises and led me to take on the part I did — besides fooling me into the delusion that it was a choice I made by my own unbiased free will and discriminating judgment.

The chief of these motives was the overwhelming idea of the great whale himself. A monster so ominous and mysterious stirred all my curiosity. Then there were the wild, far-off seas where he rolled his island-sized bulk; the untold, nameless dangers of the whale; these, together with all the marvels that come with a thousand Patagonian sights and sounds, helped push me toward what I wanted. For other men, perhaps, such things would have been no attraction at all; but as for me, I am tormented by a never-ending itch for faraway things. I love to sail forbidden seas and land on barbarous coasts. I don't overlook what is good, but I'm quick to spot a horror, and I could still be on social terms with it — if they would let me — since it's only sensible to be friendly with all the inmates of the place you're lodging in.

For all these reasons, the whaling voyage was welcome. The great floodgates of the wonder-world swung open, and in the wild fantasies that drove me toward my purpose, two by two there floated into my deepest soul endless processions of whales — and in the middle of them all, one grand hooded phantom, like a snow hill in the air.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 1 — Anelser
paragraphs: Kald mig Ishmael. For nogle år siden — det gør ikke noget, præcis hvor mange — havde jeg næsten ingen penge i pungen og ikke noget særligt, der holdt mig fast på land, og jeg besluttede mig for at sejle lidt rundt og se den vandige del af verden. Det er min måde at jage tungsindet væk på og holde blodomløbet i gang. Hver gang jeg mærker, at min mund strammer sig til en bister streg; hver gang det er en fugtig, støvregnsgrå november i min sjæl; hver gang jeg opdager, at jeg uden at ville det standser foran ligkistelagre og slentrer med bagest i hvert eneste ligfølge, jeg møder; og frem for alt hver gang mit dårlige humør tager et sådant tag i mig, at kun et stærkt moralsk princip forhindrer mig i at gå bevidst ud på gaden og systematisk slå hatten af folk — så ved jeg, at det er på høje tid at komme til søs så hurtigt, jeg kan. Det er min erstatning for pistol og kugle. Cato kaster sig med en filosofisk gestus på sit sværd; jeg går stille og roligt til søs. Der er ikke noget mærkeligt i det. Hvis de bare vidste det, ville næsten alle mennesker, hver i sin grad, på et eller andet tidspunkt føle næsten nøjagtig det samme over for havet, som jeg gør.

Der ligger så jeres ø-by Manhattoes, omgjordet af kajer, som de indiske øer er af koralrev — handelen omgiver den med sin brænding. Til højre og venstre fører gaderne dig ned mod vandet. Det yderste punkt i den nedre del af byen er Battery, hvor den ædle mole, eller havdæmning, skylles af bølger og luftes af en brise, som få timer tidligere var uden for synsvidde af land. Se på mængderne af vandskuere, der står dér.

Gå en tur rundt i byen en drømmende søndag eftermiddag. Gå fra Corlears Hook til Coenties Slip og så mod nord forbi Whitehall. Hvad ser du? Rundt om hele byen står der som tavse vagtposter tusinder på tusinder af dødelige mennesker, fortabt i havdrømme. Nogle læner sig op ad pælene; nogle sidder på enden af molerne; nogle kigger ud over rælingen på skibe fra Kina; nogle sidder højt oppe i rigningen, som om de prøvede at få et endnu bedre udsyn over havet. Men det er alle sammen landkrabber — hverdage er de spærret inde mellem puds og træ, lænket til skranker, naglet til bænke, fastspændt til skriveborde. Hvad er det, der foregår? Er alle de grønne marker forsvundet? Hvad laver de her?

Men se! Der kommer flere mængder, som går lige mod vandet og tilsyneladende vil ud at springe. Mærkeligt! Intet andet tilfredsstiller dem end selve det yderste bryn af landet; at drive om i den skyggefulde læ bag de pakhuse derovre er ikke nok. Nej. De må komme lige så tæt på vandet, som de overhovedet kan, uden at falde i. Og dér står de — flere engelske mil af dem — ja, mil på mil. Alle er de indlandsfolk, de kommer fra stræder og smug, gader og avenuer — nord, øst, syd og vest. Alligevel forenes de alle her. Sig mig, er det kompasnålenes magnetiske kraft i alle de skibe, der trækker dem hertil?

Endnu et eksempel. Sig, at du er ude på landet, et sted i et højtliggende søland. Tag næsten hvilken som helst sti, du lyster, og ti mod én fører den dig ned i en dal og efterlader dig ved et dybt kulp i åen. Der er noget magisk i det. Tag det mest distræte menneske i live, sunket i sin dybeste dagdrøm — stil ham på benene, få hans fødder i gang, og han vil føre dig til vand uden fejl, hvis der overhovedet er vand i hele egnen. Hvis du nogensinde bliver tørstig i den store amerikanske ørken, så prøv det forsøg, forudsat at din karavane tilfældigvis har en professor i metafysik med. Ja, som alle ved, er eftertanke og vand forenet for bestandig.

Men her er en maler. Han vil male dig det mest drømmende, skyggefulde, stille og fortryllende stykke romantisk landskab i hele Saco-dalen. Hvad er det vigtigste, han bygger på? Der er hans træer, hvert med en hul stamme, som om en eneboer og et krucifiks var skjult indeni; her sover hans eng, og dér sover hans kvæg; og fra det hus i det fjerne stiger en søvnig røg op. En snoet sti slynger sig dybt ind i fjerne skove og strækker sig mod overlappende bjergudløbere, badet i skråningernes blå. Men selv om billedet ligger dér i sin trance, og selv om fyrretræet her lader sine suk falde som blade ned over denne hyrdes hoved, ville det hele være forgæves, hvis ikke hyrdens blik var rettet mod den magiske strøm foran ham. Besøg præriene i juni, når du i snesevis af engelske mil vader knædybt gennem tigerliljer — hvad er den ene charme, der mangler? Vand — der er ikke en dråbe vand dér! Hvis Niagara kun var et vandfald af sand, ville du så rejse dine tusind engelske mil for at se det? Hvorfor tøvede den stakkels digter fra Tennessee, da han pludselig kom til to håndfulde sølv, om han skulle købe sig en frakke, som han trængte hårdt til, eller bruge pengene på en vandretur til Rockaway Beach? Hvorfor bliver næsten enhver stærk, rask dreng med en stærk, rask sjæl i sig på et tidspunkt splittergal efter at komme til søs? Hvorfor følte du, på din egen første rejse som passager, sådan en mystisk gysen, da man første gang fortalte dig, at du og dit skib nu var uden for synsvidde af land? Hvorfor betragtede de gamle persere havet som hellig? Hvorfor gav grækerne det en gud for sig selv og gjorde ham til Jupiters egen bror? Det er bestemt ikke uden betydning. Og dybere endnu er betydningen i historien om Narcissus, som ikke kunne gribe det plagsomme, milde billede, han så i kilden, og styrtede ud i den og druknede. Men vi ser selv det samme billede i hver flod og hvert hav. Det er billedet af livets ugribelige genfærd; og det er nøglen til det hele.

Når jeg nu siger, at jeg går til søs, hver gang mine øjne bliver tåget og jeg bliver for bevidst om min egen vejrtrækning, så forestil dig ikke, at jeg nogensinde tager af sted som passager. For at være passager skal man have en pung, og en pung er bare en klud, medmindre der er noget i den. Desuden bliver passagerer søsyge, bliver trættekære, sover ikke om natten og har generelt ikke det store udbytte af turen. Nej, jeg tager aldrig af sted som passager; og selv om jeg kender til skibe, tager jeg heller aldrig af sted som kommandør, kaptajn eller kok. Hæderen og anseelsen ved den slags poster overlader jeg til dem, der vil have dem. Personligt foragter jeg alt hæderligt, respektabelt arbejde, alle prøvelser og trængsler af enhver art. Jeg har rigeligt at gøre med bare at passe på mig selv, uden også at passe på skibe, barker, brigger, skonnerter og hvad der ellers findes. Og hvad det angår at tage af sted som kok — selv om jeg indrømmer, at der er stor hæder i det, for en kok er en slags officer om bord — så har jeg på en eller anden måde aldrig brudt mig om tanken om at grille kyllinger. Men når de først er grillet, rigtigt smurt med smør og klogt saltet og peberet, er der ingen, der taler om en grillet kylling med større respekt — ja, ærbødighed — end jeg. Det er på grund af de gamle egypteres afgudsdyrkende forkærlighed for grillet ibis og stegt flodhest, at man finder mumier af de dyr i deres enorme bagerier, pyramiderne.

Nej, når jeg går til søs, tager jeg af sted som almindelig matros, lige for masten, ned i mandskabsrummet og op til den øverste mastetop. Det er rigtigt, at de kommanderer mig rundt og får mig til at springe fra rå til rå som en græshoppe på en maienge. I begyndelsen er den slags ubehageligt nok. Det svier på stoltheden, især hvis man kommer fra en gammel, etableret familie — Van Rensselaerne eller Randolpherne eller Hardicanuterne. Og endnu mere, hvis man, lige før man stak hånden ned i tjærespanden, havde spillet herre som landsbylærer og fået de højeste drenge til at skælve for sig. Overgangen fra skolemester til sømand er brat, det forsikrer jeg dig, og kræver en solid dosis Seneca og stoikerne for at hjælpe en til at bide tænderne sammen og smile. Men også det går over med tiden.

Hvad så, om en sur gammel søkaptajn beordrer mig til at hente en kost og feje dækkene? Hvad er den ydmygelse værd, vejet, mener jeg, på Det Nye Testamentes vægtskåle? Tror du, ærkeenglen Gabriel tænker det mindste ringere om mig, fordi jeg prompte og respektfuldt adlyder den gamle gnavpot i netop det tilfælde? Hvem er ikke slave? Sig mig det. Nå, men uanset hvordan de gamle søkaptajner kommanderer med mig — uanset hvordan de puffer og slår mig rundt — så har jeg den tilfredsstillelse at vide, at det er helt i orden; at alle andre behandles på nogenlunde samme måde, på den ene eller anden måde — set fra et fysisk eller et metafysisk synspunkt, vel at mærke; og sådan bliver det universelle puf givet videre, og alle mand burde gnide hinandens skulderblade og være tilfredse.

Desuden går jeg altid til søs som matros, fordi de gør sig umage for at betale mig for min ulejlighed, mens de, så vidt jeg nogensinde har hørt, aldrig betaler passagerer et eneste øre. Tværtimod — passagerer må selv betale. Og der er hele verdens forskel på at betale og at blive betalt. At betale er måske den ubehageligste straf, som de to æbletyve, Adam og Eva, har efterladt os. Men at blive betalt — hvad kan måle sig med det? Den elskværdige beredvillighed, hvormed et menneske tager imod penge, er virkelig bemærkelsesværdig, når man tænker på, hvor inderligt vi tror, at penge er roden til alt ondt på jorden, og at en mand med penge under ingen omstændigheder kan komme i himlen. Åh, hvor muntert vi skriver os over til fortabelsen!

Endelig går jeg altid til søs som matros på grund af den sunde motion og den rene luft på bakken. For ligesom der i denne verden er langt flere modvinde end vinde agterfra (det vil sige, hvis man aldrig bryder Pythagoras' leveregel), sådan får kommandøren på agterdækket for det meste sin luft på anden hånd fra matroserne på bakken. Han tror, at han trækker den ind først; men sådan er det ikke. På omtrent samme måde går almindelige mennesker foran deres ledere i mange andre ting, mens lederne næsten ikke aner det. Men hvorfor det var, at jeg, efter gentagne gange at have lugtet til havet som handelsmatros, nu skulle få det indfald at tage med på en hvalfangerrejse — det kan skæbnens usynlige politibetjent, som holder mig under stadig overvågning, i al hemmelighed følger mine fodspor og på en eller anden uforklarlig måde påvirker mig, svare bedre på end nogen anden. Og uden tvivl var min rejse på hvalfangst en del af Forsynets store program, der blev lagt for lang tid siden. Den kom ind som en slags kort mellemakt og solo mellem større forestillinger. Jeg går ud fra, at den del af programmet må have lydt omtrent sådan:
»STORT OMSTRIDT VALG TIL DE FORENEDE STATERS PRÆSIDENTEMBEDE.« »HVALFANGERREJSE VED EN VIS ISHMAEL.« »BLODIG KAMP I AFGHANISTAN.«

Selv om jeg ikke kan sige præcis hvorfor de sceneinstruktører, skæbnegudinderne, gav mig den lurvede rolle i en hvalfangerrejse, mens andre fik prangende roller i høje tragedier, korte og lette roller i fine komedier og muntre roller i farcer — selv om jeg ikke kan sige præcis hvorfor; så synes jeg nu, når jeg husker alle omstændighederne, at jeg kan se lidt ind i de fjedre og motiver, som blev snedigt præsenteret for mig i forskellige forklædninger og fik mig til at tage den rolle på mig, jeg gjorde — foruden at narre mig til den vildfarelse, at det var et valg, jeg traf af min egen uhildede frie vilje og dømmekraft.

Det vigtigste af disse motiver var den overvældende tanke om selve den store hval. Et så uhyggeligt og mystisk uhyre vakte al min nysgerrighed. Så var der de vilde, fjerne have, hvor han væltede sin østore krop rundt; hvalens ufortalte, navnløse farer; alt dette sammen med alle de undere, der følger med tusind patagoniske syn og lyde, hjalp med at skubbe mig mod det, jeg ville. For andre mænd ville den slags måske slet ikke have været nogen tiltrækning; men hvad mig angår, plages jeg af en uophørlig kløe efter fjerne ting. Jeg elsker at sejle på forbudte have og lande på barbariske kyster. Jeg overser ikke det gode, men jeg er hurtig til at få øje på en rædsel, og jeg kunne sagtens stadig være på omgangsfod med den — hvis de ville lade mig — for det er jo bare fornuftigt at være venlig med alle beboerne på det sted, man bor.

Af alle disse grunde var hvalfangerrejsen velkommen. Vidunderverdenens store sluser svingede op, og i de vilde fantasier, der drev mig mod mit mål, flød der to og to ind i min dybeste sjæl endeløse optog af hvaler — og midt i dem alle ét stort hætteklædt genfærd, som en snebakke i luften.
